Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: The memory of the bombing on the third day of the conflict in Aleppo still clings to Ahmad like soot on his hands. He had been part of a relief team that was suddenly thrust into a makeshift morgue beside a collapsed school. The building's roof had collapsed, trapping hundreds of civilians under twisted steel and the acrid taste of scorched plaster filled the air. Ahmad recalls the heat of the blast, the metallic tang of blood, and the shuddering silence that followed the last of the sirens, a silence that still feels like a prelude to danger. When he later recounts the story to a colleague, the words are sharp and fragmented; the picture that emerges is never continuous, but jagged slices of terror that leave him gasping. He feels as if the terror is present every time he hears the distant echo of a gunshot or a muffled explosion, and he stops breathing until the threat feels distant enough to be safe. The first time he heard a stranger ask a question about the war during a town hall meeting, the memory surged in him so violently that he had to pause and swallow. In that instant the thought that he might be a target again pushed him to force himself to ignore the rawness of his emotions, to control the tremor in his voice as he responded. He began to let his eyes dart from the speaker's podium to the wall of photographs that catalogued the conflict, a distraction that kept him from focusing on the pain. This same strategy unfolded at night, when the sound of a distant motor outside his apartment, or a sudden hush in the hallway, made him feel the same urgency to shut down his feelings and redirect his mind toward the endless list of tasks that would keep his political career moving forward. Whenever a stranger approached him in a lobby, his mind would flash back to the bomb's explosion, and the only way he found to cope was to keep his emotions at bay, to keep himself busy. He has built a fortress of rituals around his living space. The heavy wooden door on his apartment is locked at all times; he feels compelled to re-check it repeatedly, to make sure that no one could come in and bring the threat that had once lived in the collapsed building. The quiet that follows is not relief but a hollow, unthreatening sound that reminds him that he has control, that he has closed the door. Yet when he hears the hiss of a lock that seems to be already secure, the memory of the building's silent aftermath flares again, reminding him that the silence could mean a new threat is looming. The checking becomes a way to counter the threat of silence, but at the same time the act of checking re-ignites the memory, making him feel as if the danger is still present. He has also begun to scan the windows at night, looking for any movement that might suggest an intruder, the same way he scanned the alley in Aleppo for hidden mortar pits. The scanning keeps him in a constant state of alertness, a state that is both a response to the memory and a trigger for the memory to surface again. His career as a state senator keeps him in perpetual contact with strangers. In the morning he greets constituents, in the afternoon he attends committee hearings where the topic of military policy is often raised. Every time a veteran speaks about a deployment, the memory of the blast re-ignites, the smell of burned concrete drifting from the air of the Senate chamber, and his heart begins to pound. To keep himself from unraveling, he overworks, pushing himself to prepare speeches, to write policy briefs, to review case files until his eyes blur. The work is an attempt to distract, but the very act of working reminds him of the urgency to keep moving, to keep his life on schedule, a schedule that keeps the memory in a loop of constant activation. The constant motion keeps him from confronting the terror, but the terror still follows him to the conference room, to the quiet lobby, and to the kitchen of his office where he pours coffee in a rhythm that feels like a ritual. In the past year, his avoidance has begun to take a tangible toll. He has stopped attending the weekly community garden where he used to meet with local activists, citing a need to avoid strangers in a noisy environment. He no longer speaks up in council meetings, fearing that the conversation might turn to war, that the memory will surface and overwhelm him. He has begun to keep a stack of legal briefs on his desk that he never reads, a symbolic gesture of overwork that provides him an excuse to remain in his office and to stay away from the unpredictability of the outside world. The isolation is compounded by the fact that his divorce left him with no one who could sit beside him and help him articulate the fear that he cannot bear to speak aloud. His fear of the memory resurfacing in the middle of a quiet moment, the feeling that the silence itself is a threat, keeps him locked in his office, his eyes glued to the glowing screen of his laptop, his mind racing with imagined danger. The day he finally decided to see a therapist was when a sudden, inexplicable bout of panic struck him during a televised debate. His throat closed, his vision tunneled, and the taste of burnt metal returned in his mouth. He could not finish his sentence and had to leave the room before his colleagues could finish their questions. The episode left him feeling utterly exposed and powerless. The fear that this could happen again, that he might lose his composure on public stage or in private conversation, spurred him to seek help. He hopes to learn to breathe without feeling that a door is ajar, to understand why a quiet hallway feels like a prelude to a bomb, and to rebuild a life where the past does not dictate the present.
